beginner.headline: Japan plans mission to get dust from a Mars moon
beginner.brief: A space mission will launch soon to visit a moon of Mars. The spacecraft will leave from Japan and arrive at the moon in 2027. A small robot will look for a safe place to land. The spacecraft will touch down on the surface and grab some dust. A small capsule will bring this dust back to Earth in 2031. Scientists hope the dust will explain how the moons of Mars formed. The spacecraft will bring back only a tiny amount of material. Even a small amount is enough to learn more about space.

intermediate.headline: Mars Mission Aims to Bring Moon Dust Back to Earth
intermediate.brief: A new mission will attempt to grab a piece of a Martian moon and bring it back to Earth. The project plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat. The strong gravity of nearby Mars makes it much harder to get a rover onto the moon's surface. Once on the surface, the vehicle will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some dust. This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031. Scientists can conduct several studies even on individual grains, so they do not need to bring back kilograms of rock. Researchers believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from. The results will quickly show whether the moon is the product of a dramatic impact or a captured asteroid. Because the moon is so close to Mars, the returned sample may actually contain grains from the planet itself.

advanced.headline: Japan Aims to Retrieve Pristine Dust from Martian Moon Phobos
advanced.brief: A pioneering space expedition is scheduled to depart on Monday, embarking on an ambitious endeavor to retrieve material from Mars' moon Phobos. The bold initiative, spearheaded by the Japanese Space Agency, aims to resolve the enduring mystery surrounding the formation of these Martian satellites. The automated rover will scout out a suitable location so that the main probe can subsequently touch down securely. Landing on such a small celestial body poses a formidable challenge because its remarkably weak gravity is dwarfed by that of the adjacent planet. The collected material will be securely packed for transit, culminating in a 2031 descent into the Australian desert. Experts stress that such a minuscule quantity provides ample material for comprehensive laboratory studies, proving that massive amounts are unnecessary. Scientists anticipate that examining the chemistry and mineral composition will produce distinct results to evaluate the conflicting hypotheses. Furthermore, experts harbor hopes that proximity has allowed ejected grains from the Martian crust to become embedded directly into Phobos. This could provide unprecedented, direct information regarding the chemical makeup and geological history of Mars itself. Securing uncontaminated matter is paramount for researchers, as existing Martian meteorites inevitably suffer terrestrial contamination upon atmospheric entry.
